en: Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya || Homage to the Blessed Buddha!

Desiring to compose the *Madhyamakāvatāra* (The Entrance to the Middle Way) for the purpose of introducing the *Madhyamakaśāstra*, [the author] first [praises] the Blessed One’s Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is the primary cause for the attainment of Buddhahood and is characterized by the protection of unprotected sentient beings imprisoned within the prison of the entirety of saṃsāra; [he praises it] as well as the Perfectly Awakened Ones and the Bodhisattvas.
Establishing his worthiness for praise, he speaks these two verses:
The Śrāvakas are born from the Lord of Munis, and the Buddhas arise from the Bodhisattvas;
Compassionate mind, non-dual wisdom, and the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta) are the causes of the Sons of the Conquerors.

And so forth. In this context, because they are endowed with the perfection of sovereignty over unsurpassed dharmas—and thus possess a supreme sovereignty even compared to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—and because śrāvakas and others abide under the power of their command, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are called "Lords of Munis" (munīndra). Those born from them are "born of the Lords of Munis" (munīndraja), namely the śrāvakas.

The [consonants] beginning with *ka*. How so? Because when Buddhas appear, there occurs the teaching of unerring dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); and through the sequence of hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on that, disciples and others achieve full realization according to their respective inclinations. Even though the instruction on dependent origination—

Even those who have attained the hearing of the ultimate truth through listening do not, in some cases, realize nirvāṇa in this very life. Nevertheless, just as with karma whose ripening is fixed, the teachers of that instruction will inevitably attain the fruition of their desired result in another birth.
As the noble Āryadeva has said:
"In this world, even if one who knows reality does not attain nirvāṇa,
he will certainly obtain it without effort in a future birth, just like [the ripening of] karma."

Thus it is said. For this very reason, it is also stated in the *Madhyamaka*: "In the absence of the appearance of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and upon the passing away of the Śrāvakas, the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from non-association."

Thus, they are called *śrāvakas* because they cause others to hear the fruit of correct instruction (*samyagavavāda*). For instance: "What was to be done has been done; we recognize no further existence beyond this," and so forth.

Alternatively, they are called *śrāvakas* because, having heard from the Tathāgatas the supreme fruit or the path of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they cause those who seek that same goal to hear it.

They go [to nirvana], thus they are called *śrāvakas*. As it is said in the noble *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "O Protector, today we have become *śrāvakas*; we shall proclaim the supreme enlightenment (*agrabodhi*) and make known the sound of enlightenment to you..."

Just as water is of primary utility at the beginning, middle, and end of the preparation of medicinal decoctions (*jalapāka*), so too does this illustrate that compassion is useful for the harvest of the Victors' grain throughout all three times. For one who possesses compassion, being pained by the suffering of others, is necessarily committed to the protection of all sentient beings who are suffering.

He generates the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), thinking: "This entire world must necessarily be rescued by me from suffering and established in Buddhahood. And this vow cannot be accomplished unless non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*) is realized; therefore, he necessarily applies himself even toward non-dual knowledge. From this [arises] compassion...
It is not at all the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha. As it has been said:
"All movements preceded by compassion and purified by wisdom—what conscious person would disparage that Mahāyāna in which they are taught?"

Thus, even if one has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), if one does not repeatedly receive the sprinkling of the water of compassion at subsequent times, it is certain that this person— failing to accumulate a vast store of fruit— will be extinguished by the parinirvāṇa of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. [But] having attained the infinite fruits...
Even if one were established [in that state], if one were devoid of the ripening of compassion, this would not be enjoyed for a long time;
nor would the great accumulation of noble fruits, proceeding in an uninterrupted succession, increase for long.
Now, having illuminated the excellence of the nature of compassion even through its engagement with specific objects, he speaks, desiring to begin his salutation to it:
"When 'I' was previously established in the self, and attachment to existence [expressed as] 'this is mine' had been instilled..."
I bow to that compassion which arose for this world, which is as lacking in autonomy as a revolving water-wheel.
Even before the attachment to "mine" (*ātmīyābhiniveśa*), one imagines through the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) that a non-existent self exists;

thus, being attached to this as true, the entire world is attached to the collection of phenomena other than the object of the ego-sense, thinking "this is mine. And this [world] is thus attached to the self and what belongs to the self.

The world is bound very tightly by the rope of karma and afflictions; its functioning is dependent on the driving force of the mechanism of consciousness. From the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, it is incessantly driven into the great pit of saṃsāra. Tending naturally toward downward movement, it can only be raised up with great effort, for it is [driven] by ignorance.
Even within the threefold defilement of afflictions, karma, and birth, the sequence of beginning, middle, and end cannot be determined;

because it is shattered day after day by the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change, it remains in a state that does not transcend the condition of a waterwheel’s buckets. Out of compassion for the suffering of those [beings], the Bodhisattva—

Because he strives to protect him by relying upon supreme compassion, he first of all paid homage to the Blessed Lady, Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). And this is the compassion of Bodhisattvas that has sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambanā karuṇā*).
Demonstrating that compassion has both a focal object (*sālambana*) and no focal object (*anālambana*) by way of its very object, he says:

"I bow to that compassion of one who perceives the world as flickering like the moon in water that ripples at its edges, and as empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnya*). For thus, in water that is extremely clear...
When the reflection of the internal moon— its parts being stirred by a wind that is not too violent—

spreads forth and perishes simultaneously with its previously perceived substratum, the wise perceive these two things as existing together, as if their own self-nature were manifesting right before them, appearing as if it were arising to perception. That is to say:

[They perceive] momentary impermanence and the emptiness of intrinsic nature. In this way, Bodhisattvas also see sentient beings— who dwell within the vast, dark blue waters of ignorance, tossed by the winds of improper conceptualization in the lake of the view of a self-existent body— as if they were the reflections of their own karma appearing right before them.

In order to attain Buddhahood— which is characterized by the cessation of all erroneous conceptualizations, which has as its nature friendship toward the entire world, and which is the cause for drinking the supreme nectar of the True Dharma as if it were the remedy for the affliction of that very impermanence; [Buddhahood] which is empty of intrinsic nature and yet, moment by moment, is struck down by the calamity of impermanence— [he strives].
Those who are dependent on compassion desire [to act].

Having paid homage to those compassions of theirs which have sentient beings as their object, phenomena as their object, and no object, [the author], desiring to explain the tenfold division of the bodhicitta of Bodhisattvas, first speaks with reference to that initial bodhicitta:
Independent of [self-interest] through compassion for the sake of the liberation of all worlds, it is directed by the vows of Samantabhadra.
That mind of the Son of the Conqueror which is established in sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is called the first [stage].

For it is the very wisdom of the Bodhisattvas, embraced by compassion and the like, which—being untainted (*anāsrava*) and analyzed into its parts—receives the designation of "stages" (*bhūmi*), because it serves as the foundation for qualities. And that [wisdom] is progressively...

It is established as tenfold according to the divisions of the stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), due to the distinctions in the excellence of the attainment of the qualities of faith, the number [of perfections], and the power [of those perfections], as well as the preeminence of the maturation resulting from the superiority of the perfections such as giving (*dāna*). However, there is no distinction made on account of any excellence in its essential nature (*svarūpa*). As it has been said:
Just as the track of a bird in the sky cannot be described or seen by the Buddhas,
even so all the stages of the Sons of the Conquerors cannot be described, much less heard.

Thus it is said. In that regard, the Bodhisattva stage called *pramuditā* (the Joyous) is the first production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) for Bodhisattvas, up to the tenth production of the thought of awakening, which is *dharmameghā* (the Cloud of Dharma). Therein, according to the principle already stated, for the Bodhisattva who perceives the world as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) and who has embraced compassion as a specific qualification, that which...

The mind, independent of compassion, dedicated through the vows of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, is the non-dual gnosis named "Great Joy" (*pramuditā*), characterized by its causal signs and fruits; that is called the first [stage]. Therein, for the Bodhisattva, there are ten vows, headed by the ten great vows.

The hundreds of thousands of incalculable aspirations that a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening produces are all included within the vow of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The specific mention of Samantabhadra’s vow is for the purpose of encompassing every aspiration without exception. In this regard, just as...

In the Śrāvakayāna, eight śrāvaka-bhūmis are established based on the distinction between the stages of practicing and attaining the fruits. Likewise, in the Mahāyāna, there are ten bodhisattva-bhūmis for bodhisattvas. Furthermore, a śrāvaka who has arisen in the stage of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) is not at all in the stage of practicing for the first fruit.

It is accepted that such is the future bodhisattva. As it is stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*: "That state immediately preceding the attainment of the first stage, by virtue of the nature of the practice of superior resolve (*adhimukti*), is called the 'stage of the bodhisattva who has not yet generated the thought of awakening' (*anutpāditabodhicitta-bhūmi*). That resolve—

And the state of the *vyākṣaṇa* is explained in that very same place: "For example, noble son, just as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) has transcended human complexion but has not yet attained divine complexion;
even so, the bodhisattva has transcended all worldly [complexion]..."
He has not yet attained the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, nor the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva.
However, when he enters the first stage called Pramuditā (the Joyous),
from that point onward, he is indeed designated by the very term "Bodhisattva" by virtue of his attainment.

In every respect, one who has attained that mind should be designated by the very term "bodhisattva" during the state of having transcended the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and not otherwise, because at that time he is a noble one (*ārya*). As it is said in the *Bhagavatī* in two thousand five hundred verses: "Bodhisattva" is a designation for a being who has followed after awakening.
Homage! By whom all phenomena have been fully awakened to and known. How are they known? As non-existent, unarisen, and unreal;
they are not as they are imagined by foolish common people; they are not as they are apprehended by foolish common people. For that reason, one is called a "bodhisattva. Why is that?

For awakening is non-conceptual; for awakening is unconstructed; for awakening is non-apprehensible. Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, no awakening was attained by the Tathāgata, because of the non-attainment of all dharmas. Because of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, it is called "awakening."
Thus indeed is it called the awakening of a Buddha; but it is not as it is described by those who, having generated the thought of awakening, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, think:
"We shall generate this thought for the sake of awakening," or who imagine that awakening exists—that awakening for which we shall generate the thought.

"May we become [Buddhas]," they say. They are not called Bodhisattvas; rather, they are called "beings who have arisen. For what reason? Because, being attached to arising and attached to the mind, they become attached to awakening, and so forth. Furthermore, it has been said: "Awakening is indeed without characteristics (*alakṣaṇā*); [it is] characteristic—"

That which is the turning away from intrinsic nature—this very awakening is called "bodhi. It is not, however, as it is commonly expressed. For, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, because he has awakened to these dharmas, one is called a "bodhisattva.
Indeed, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever does not understand these dharmas...

If a Bodhisattva who is not awakening claims for himself, "I am a Bodhisattva," his Bodhisattva-stage is far away; he is far from the qualities of a Bodhisattva. He deceives the world of gods, humans, and asuras by means of the name "Bodhisattva. If, O Suvikrāntavikrāmin...
If a bodhisattva were to exist by mere words, then all sentient beings would also be bodhisattvas. However,
O Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this so-called "bodhisattva stage" is not merely a matter of verbal action,
and so forth.
Not only is one who has obtained the aforementioned bodhicitta described by the very term "bodhisattva" in that state, but moreover,
he is born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
All three of his fetters have been destroyed,
for he has acquired the power to shake a hundred world-systems.

Because he has completely transcended the stages of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, and because he has generated the path that follows the stage of the Tathāgata called "Universal Radiance" (*samantaprabhā*), the bodhisattva is born into the family of the Tathāgatas.

This is due to his direct perception of selflessness within himself, [which abandons] the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and [wrong] views regarding ethical discipline (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
At that time, even his three fetters known as the attachment to vows have vanished due to their non-recurrence.

For one who does not see reality, the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) would arise from the superimposition of a self; likewise, it is possible for such a person to deviate toward another path due to doubt. This is not the case for anyone else—namely, for one who has entered the state of certainty (*niyāma*).

And because of that progress, through the attainment of qualities that are its cause, through the departure from the defects that are the adversaries of the stage, and through the arising of a special, uncommon joy, that bodhisattva, owing to an abundance of gladness, bears supreme delight. And because of the presence of this distinguished delight, this stage receives the name "The Joyous" (*pramuditā*). Śa—
And he can cause a hundred world-systems to tremble with a single knot.
Then he ascends from the world to the world above, taking up the higher realms;
at that time, every path to the lower states is blocked for him,
and all the levels of ordinary beings are exhausted for him.
This noble one has been taught in the same manner as the eighth-rank practitioner.
By means of the complete mastery of the Dharma as it has been realized, and because of his great enthusiasm for entering the second and subsequent stages,

he proceeds upward, traversing stage after stage. In brief, just as for a noble one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), there is the disappearance of faults and the arising of qualities due to the realization of the noble dharmas corresponding to his own level, so too—
Furthermore, the arising of qualities in one's own form and the exhaustion of faults resulting from this bodhisattva’s attainment of the stages are illustrated by the analogy of the stream-enterer.
And this is another distinction: that this Bodhisattva,
by the sovereign power of his merit, increases as he surpasses even the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the voice of the Lord of Sages,
for he does so even while established in the first thought of awakening.

As it is said in the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa*: "Just as, noble son, a newborn prince, though endowed with the marks of royalty, surpasses all the senior ministers who have reached the pinnacle of their careers by virtue of his family’s majesty and sovereignty; even so, one who has newly generated the thought of awakening [surpasses others] through the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma..."

A beginner bodhisattva who has not yet been reborn [in the higher realms] surpasses śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have long practiced the holy life through the sovereign power of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Son of good family, it is just as, for example, the strength, power, and prowess of the wing-wind of a newly born young of the great king of garuḍas [surpasses that of other birds].

And there is the quality of the purity of his vision, which does not exist among all other flocks of birds that have grown to full size in their bodies. In the very same way, the [vision] of omniscience belonging to a Bodhisattva, who is like a great garuḍa prince born from the lineage of the great garuḍa king Tathāgata, as soon as he first produces the thought of awakening—

The power and prowess of generating [this] and the quality of the complete purification of the eye of resolute intention do not exist even among all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have emerged over hundreds of thousands of eons, and so forth.
But by means of a mind that has gone far, he is even more distinguished.

As it is said in the *Āryadaśabhūmika*: "O sons of the Conqueror, it is just as if a prince born into a royal family, endowed with the marks of royalty, would, immediately upon birth, surpass the entire assembly of ministers by virtue of his royal sovereignty, yet not by the power of his own intellectual deliberation. When..."

Furthermore, as he grows, he then surpasses all the activities of the ministers by virtue of the empowerment of his own intelligence. In the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva, from the mere arising of the thought of enlightenment, surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas through the greatness of his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*). Yet, not...
By means of investigating with the power of his own intellect, a bodhisattva established on this seventh bodhisattva-ground,

because he abides in the majesty of the knowledge of his own domain, transcends all the activities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Thus, from the ground Dūraṅgamā onwards, by means of his own intellect—

Even by means of slight effort, a bodhisattva surpasses the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this should be understood as applying to those on the lower stages. Precisely from this scripture, it is clearly determined that even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the knowledge of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanaiḥsvābhāvya*). Otherwise, [if they lacked] the selflessness of phenomena...

Because they lack a thorough understanding of that which is to be cultivated, even those [śrāvakas] would be surpassed by a bodhisattva at the very first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpādika), even through the latter’s own intellectual investigation; furthermore, like outsiders, they would not achieve the abandonment of all latent tendencies (anuśaya) pertaining to the three realms. This is because they perceive the intrinsic nature of form and the other aggregates.

It is not so, because it would be erroneous; even the realization of selflessness regarding the self would not occur, since there would still be the perception of the aggregates that serve as the basis for the designation of a "self. As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, to that same extent there is also the notion of 'I'."
When there is egoism, there is again action, and from that, birth once more.
This wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of the three paths, is without beginning, middle, or end;
resembling a whirling circle of fire, it revolves with each part serving as the cause for the other.
Because self, other, and both are not found in the three times, the ego-sense comes to an end; and with it, karma and birth.
Thus it is said again:
"Just as the eye perceives a circle of fire due to a cognitive error,
so too do the sense faculties perceive objects as if they were present."
The sense faculties and the objects of the sense faculties are considered to be composed of the five elements;
since each individual element is redundant, these [faculties and objects] are in fact devoid of purpose.

If there were no distinction between the elements, it would follow that fire exists without fuel; if there were contact, there would be an absence of defining characteristics. This same conclusion applies to the remaining [elements] as well.
Thus, since both types of elements are purposeless, their conjunction is also in vain;
and because their conjunction is purposeless, form is therefore purposeless in reality.
Furthermore, because the self is individually redundant in relation to consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations, they are all ultimately redundant in every respect.
Just as the conceit of happiness regarding the remedy for suffering is not true in reality,
so too is the conceit of suffering born from the obstruction of pleasure.

Thus, through the lack of intrinsic nature, the thirst for union with pleasure is abandoned; likewise, the thirst for separation from suffering is abandoned. For one who sees this, there is liberation.
If it is asked, "Who sees?", it is said, by way of conventional usage, that it is the mind (*citta*).
For there is no mind without mental factors (*caitta*); since [the mind] would otherwise be purposeless, it will not exist [as such].
Having thus understood the world to be futile according to its true nature, one who is without support becomes extinguished,
like a fire without fuel, being devoid of any substratum for rebirth.

Now, it might be argued: "It is only Bodhisattvas who perceive this lack of intrinsic nature (naiḥsvābhāvya) in such a way. But this is not so, because this statement was made specifically with reference to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. If it is asked how this is known, it is said: immediately following [the previous passage], there is a reference to Bodhisattvas—
The Bodhisattva, too, having seen this, is considered certain of perfect enlightenment;
yet, out of mere compassion, his succession of births continues until awakening.

Because of such statements as these, and because in the *Śrāvakopadeśa-sūtras* the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are described through similes such as a lump of foam, a water bubble, a mirage, the water of a mirage, the trunk of a plantain tree, and an illusion, for the sake of the Śrāvakas' abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a bubble; perception is similar to a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree,
and consciousness is said by the Kinsman of the Sun to be like an illusion.
With these words, the Master, establishing this very point, stated:
"In the Mahāyāna, non-arising is emptiness; for others, it is cessation.
Since cessation and non-arising are identical in meaning, let this be accepted."
Likewise,
in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" were refuted by the Blessed One, who perceives both existence and non-existence.
Thus it is said.

As for the one who thinks: "If the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) were taught even in the Śrāvakayāna, then the teaching of the Mahāyāna would be rendered purposeless"—his view is likewise refuted by the following reasoning:
It is observed that [the Mahāyāna] is not devoid of a path. Nor does the teaching of the Mahāyāna establish merely the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

What then? It also establishes the inconceivable nature of reality (*dharmatā*)—including the stages (*bhūmi*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), the vows (*praṇidhāna*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the two accumulations (*sambhāra*) for the transformation [of merit] of the Bodhisattvas. As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
Neither the vow of a bodhisattva nor the dedication of conduct is taught in the Śrāvakayāna; how then could one be a bodhisattva on that basis?
The words spoken in the Sūtras were not intended for the purpose of establishing the conduct of awakening;
however, those spoken in the Mahāyāna should be accepted by the wise for that reason.

Thus, the teaching of the Mahāyāna is indeed appropriate for the purpose of illuminating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), because it is intended to provide a detailed exposition. In the Śrāvakayāna, however, there is merely an indication of the selflessness of phenomena,
as stated by the venerable Master [Vasubandhu]:
"You have stated that there is no liberation without relying on the signless;
therefore, you have taught it in its entirety within the Mahāyāna."
Thus; enough with this digression.
Therefore, it is precisely this that is being further described: those whose minds are undisturbed are themselves capable of realizing the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, the giving of that [teaching] is indeed the primary cause for the awakening of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

For that bodhisattva who has attained the stage of the Joyous (pramuditā-bhūmi), among the ten perfections known as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and primordial wisdom, it is the perfection of generosity alone that becomes predominant; yet it is not that the others are absent for him. And that generosity—
This is the first cause of omniscience.
And he was the cause for seeing what was previously unseen, even when [the Bodhisattva] was intent on giving his own flesh.

For even those qualities of a bodhisattva that are invisible, such as the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth, are at that time inferred by him even more clearly through the specific excellence of his renunciation of external and internal things— just as fire and other properties are inferred from smoke.

And just as the generosity of bodhisattvas is the primary cause of Buddhahood and a sign for determining qualities that are not perceptible, so too is it the cause for ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas to achieve the remedy for suffering and the attainment of ultimate happiness; in order to demonstrate this, he says:
All these people desire happiness, yet for humans there is no happiness without enjoyments;
and knowing that enjoyments arise from giving, [one should practice charity].
In ancient times, the Sage recounted stories of generosity.

The arising of happiness within the realms of existence is merely the alleviation of suffering. The world is deeply attached to that which is essentially devoid of happiness—a continuum of selfhood imagined through mere cognitive distortion, wherein the onset of hunger, thirst, disease, cold, and so forth is warded off by their respective remedies. And thus, for such a world, [this] happiness— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

The pleasure of those who desire, which is essentially nothing more than a remedy for suffering, is never observed to arise except through enjoyment that consists of a perversion of desired objects, serving as an antidote to suffering.

And having understood that even those sense objects which serve as remedies for suffering do not arise for those who have not accumulated the bases of meritorious action consisting of giving, the Blessed One— who knows the disposition and nature of the entire world—
delivered discourses on giving first and foremost, rather than discourses on ethical discipline and the like.
Now, even though the donor being may be deficient, he speaks in order to manifest the greatness of giving according to its own function:
"Those who are devoid of compassion have extremely harsh minds."
Even for those whose very purposes are different [from one's own],
their desired enjoyments arise from giving, for it is the primary cause for the cessation of suffering.

For even those who, like merchants, out of a desire for the fruit of accumulating a vast store of wealth by relinquishing a very small amount of capital, respect the wish to give to those who have become even more eager than ordinary supplicants; they do not, however, like the sons of the Sugata, out of dependence on compassion, bestow gifts even upon those who are not supplicants at all.

Forming bonds through their desire to give, they increase the festival of joy; yet even for them, that gift— being averted from grasping at faults and perfected by the skill of grasping only virtues— becomes a cause for the cessation of suffering, as it suppresses the physical suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth with an abundance of excellent enjoyments.
Homage!
Furthermore, he who, due to a lack of compassion, honors the desire to give solely out of regard for remedying his own suffering—
even such a person might, through attachment to giving, occasionally attain association with noble beings;
from that, having severed the蔓延 (expansion) of existence, he might even proceed to auspiciousness on that basis.

Because of the saying, "The giver and the lord of giving are followed by the virtuous," through the context of giving and association with noble persons, and by their instruction, he came to know the worthlessness of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Having abandoned ignorance (*avidyā*) and brought the stainless Noble Path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation,
he [abandoned] the expansion of cyclic existence that has proceeded from beginningless time through a succession of births and deaths.

Having abandoned [the path], one who is devoted to generosity attains parinirvāṇa by means of the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Thus, for those who are not Bodhisattvas, generosity is the cause for attaining the happiness of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Those whose minds have committed themselves to the welfare of the world obtain what is to be obtained through giving without delay.
For it has been said that non-bodhisattvas do not necessarily enjoy the fruit of giving at the same time as the act itself.
Thus, because the fruit of their giving is not manifest before them, it is even possible that they might fail to engage in giving. [This is not so for] bodhisattvas—
At the very moment of giving, because they bring satisfaction to the minds of those who seek, and because they carry joy through the excellence of the fruit of the desired gift,
they enjoy the fruit of that giving this very day; therefore, they always become fond of giving.

Thus, according to the reasoning described above, since giving is the cause of both worldly prosperity and the supreme good for all— whether they be compassionate by nature or devoid of compassion— the discourse on giving alone is the very foundation.

What indeed is the extraordinary joy that arises for Bodhisattvas when they satisfy the minds of supplicants by sharing their enjoyments, such that they always hold generosity in high esteem? It is said: "The entry into peace through the renunciation of everything brings happiness to the Sages in a way that nothing else does."
Just as the sound "Give! brings forth happiness for the sons of the Conquerors through their cultivation of the mental impression of hearing that word.

When those seeking something merely imagine hearing the sound of the word "Give," and repeatedly perceive that "these people are begging from me," the joy that arises in the Bodhisattvas is indeed superior even to the bliss of Nirvana; how much more so when they actually bestow external and internal things upon those who seek them?

"...let them lie down. But does no physical suffering arise even for those bodhisattvas who renounce internal objects as well? For this reason it is said: "Indeed, for the great-souled ones, unlike those lacking consciousness, there is no possibility of the arising of physical suffering when their bodies are being cut. Why is that? Because...
It is stated briefly in the *Āryagaganagañjasamādhi*: "For example, suppose there were a great grove of *śāla* trees.

Someone might come and cut down one *śāla* tree therein. Among the remaining *śāla* trees, it does not occur to them: 'This one has been cut down; we are not cut down. Nor do they [have such thoughts]."
It is not a method, nor is it aversion, nor conceptualization, nor discursive thought. Such patience as this is the supreme, sky-like purification of patience for a bodhisattva.
And it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
He would have no physical suffering, nor could there be any mental suffering for him;
through his compassion for the suffering of the world, he remains for a long time in that very state.
Thus [it is said].

Even for one who has not yet attained the state of non-attachment, bodily suffering necessarily arises from the encounter with sense objects that oppose the maintenance of the body; yet even that [suffering] remains as a cause for his even greater engagement in activities for the sake of sentient beings— thus he says:
Having severed his own body and giving away his own sufferings for the sake of the suffering of others— such as that of the hells—
he perceives this through direct self-awareness and swiftly exerts effort for its very severance.

Beholding with his own direct experience the suffering of those sentient beings who are obstructed by the narrow passages of the various realms of existence—such as the hells, the animal kingdom, and the world of Yama; whose bodies are being incessantly torn apart by increasingly intense sufferings; and who, while already suffering, endure unbearable pain that accumulates to a degree thousands of times greater than the pain of having their own bodies cut.
The Bodhisattva, disregarding even the pain of cutting his own body, exerts even more intense vigor for the sake of severing the sufferings of sentient beings in the hells and other realms.
Explaining the classification of the perfections (*pāramitā*) regarding the gift as it has been described, he says:
"The supramundane perfection is the gift that is empty of the object to be given, the recipient, and the giver.
In this context, *pāra* is said to be that further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, which is [the state] where the obscurations of afflictions and the known are entirely exhausted.

Buddhahood is the form of abandonment. *Pāramitā* means "gone to the further shore" (*pāram itā gatā*). By the grammatical rule *aluk-uttarapada*, the instrumental case ending is not elided (*aluk*), resulting in this form. Alternatively, by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the suffix *-m* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). The etymological derivation is based on taking *prajñā* [as the primary element]. However, generosity and the other perfections are also *pāramitās*.

Just as with the perfections (*pāramitā*), giving (*dāna*) receives the designation "perfection" because it is established as necessarily leading to the further shore through specific modes of transformation. The same should be understood for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the others that will be discussed hereafter. Furthermore, this giving, which is designated as a perfection, is [defined] by the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of the gift, the recipient, and the giver.

It is stated in the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā* that when [non-apprehension] exists, it is called a supramundane perfection (*lokottara-pāramitā*), because non-apprehension transcends the world. Since apprehension is comprised within conventional truth (*vyavahāra-satya*) and is therefore mundane, this cannot be maintained by those who have not yet attained the stage of a bodhisattva. Furthermore...
That which is free from attachment to those three is declared to be the mundane perfection (laukikī pāramitā).
That very same generosity, when there is apprehension of the three, is taught as the mundane perfection of generosity.
Now, extolling the excellence of this specific knowledge that designates the stages as previously described by way of its qualities, he says:
Established in the minds of the sons of the Conquerors, this [knowledge] triumphs, possessing the splendor of beauty acquired through its excellent support.
Having dispelled even the thickest darkness entirely, she rejoices like a moonstone at the sight of the moon.
The word *iti* is intended to indicate the manner previously described. *Muditā* is the mention of the name of the earth.

*Jayati* means that she remains having defeated her adversaries. Being established in the minds of the sons of the Victors (*jinatanaya*) and being thus situated on high because her nature is wisdom (*jñāna*), this very [joy] overcomes even dense darkness.

Having shaken off everything according to the reasoning already described, the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) triumphs. Clarifying the very meaning already described by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as the jewel of the moon," and so forth.
The first generation of the mind of awakening, titled "The Joyous," from the *Madhyamakāvatāra*.
The first production of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) of a bodhisattva has been explained. Now, with reference to the second, he says:

"Even in dreams, he is free from the stain of immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*), due to his possession of the purity of the quality of perfect morality (*śīlasampad*). Because all the specific knowledges designated as the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*) possess a single nature, morality is inseparable from them.
It is precisely through the excellence of qualities such as the perfections that he manifests the distinctions of the second and subsequent productions of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*).

In this context, because it does not tolerate the afflictions (*kleśa*) and because evil does not arise, the mind is cooled by the subsiding of the fire of remorse; or, because it is the cause of happiness and is to be practiced by the virtuous, it is called "discipline" (*śīla*). And that [discipline] is sevenfold—
The characteristic of abstention consists of three factors—non-greed, non-hatred, and right view—which are its motivators.

Thus, in the section on ethical discipline (*śīla*), the ten paths of action are explained. "Perfection of ethical discipline" (*śīlasampat*) means the excellence of ethical discipline. The analysis of the compound is: "the purity of qualities through the perfection of ethical discipline," hence "purity of qualities."

Because of the complete purity of its own qualities, ethical discipline (*śīla*) alone is preeminent. Through its application, that bodhisattva is not affected by the stains of immoral conduct even in the state of dreaming. How, then, does such a perfection of ethical discipline come to possess this purity of qualities? He says: because, on the second bodhisattva stage...
This Bodhisattva,
established with completely purified conduct of speech, body, and mind, accumulates all ten paths of wholesome action.

As it was said in the second Bodhisattvabhūmi: "In that regard, O sons of the Conqueror, a bodhisattva established in the Vimalā bodhisattvabhūmi is by his very nature abstinent from taking life; indeed, he has laid aside the rod, laid aside the weapon, and laid aside enmity."

Possessed of shame and endowed with compassion, feeling pity for the welfare and happiness of all living beings, he does not commit violence against any creature even through an unwholesome intention; how much less, then, would he intentionally inflict gross physical harm upon other beings while perceiving them as sentient beings?

Furthermore, he abstains from taking what is not given; he is content with his own possessions, has no desire for the possessions of others, and is compassionate. Regarding things possessed by others, perceiving them as belonging to others, and maintaining a mind free from theft, he does not take even a blade of grass or a leaf that has not been given. Who [is such a person]?
Furthermore, it is superior to other requisites for sustaining life.

Furthermore, he abstains from sexual misconduct; indeed, he is content with his own wife, has no longing for the wives of others, and does not give rise to covetousness toward women who are under the protection of others, who are the wives of others, or who are protected by their family, the Dharma, or the banner [of their clan]. How much less, then, would he engage in the union of the two organs or in improper conduct?
Or by means of informative action.

Furthermore, he abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, a speaker at the proper time, a speaker of what is factual, one who acts according to what he says. Even when he has gone into the midst of sleep, having set aside his view, acceptance, preference, thought, and discernment, he does not utter a false word with the intention to deceive.
O ascetic, what need is there to mention doing so intentionally?

Furthermore, he abstains from slanderous speech; indeed, he is committed to non-divisiveness and non-harming toward all sentient beings. Having heard something here, he does not report it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people. Having heard something there, he does not report it here for the purpose of dividing those people. He does not cause those who are united to be divided, nor does he...
He does not utter divisive speech; he does not delight in divisiveness, nor take pleasure in it, nor speak words that cause division—whether they be true or false.

Furthermore, he abstains from harsh speech. Such speech as this: which is rough, harsh, coarse, bitter to others, provocative of hostility, immediate, directly offensive, vulgar, characteristic of ordinary worldlings, unrefined, unpleasant to the ear, and uttered out of anger and rage.

Having abandoned such speech as burns the heart, gives rise to resentment, causes mental anguish, is unpleasant, disagreeable, and unappealing— speech that destroys one's own continuum and the continua of others— one should instead employ speech that is affectionate, gentle, pleasing, conducive to what is dear, and conducive to what is beneficial.
It was measured, pleasant to the ear, heart-stirring, lovely, urbane, distinct in its phonemes, intelligible,
worth hearing, independent, desired by many, beloved by many, dear to many,
agreeable to many, praised by the wise, bringing welfare and happiness to all beings, and composed.

She utters such speech as causes the mind to rejoice, causes the mind to be gladdened, causes one's own continuum and the continua of others to be gladdened, and pacifies all afflictions— attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Furthermore, he abstains from frivolous chatter; indeed, his speech is well-restrained.

He speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks according to the Dharma, speaks with justice, and speaks according to discipline. He utters speech that is well-founded, timely, and coherent, even down to the traditional legends.
He avoids even speech that was previously intended as an avoidance; how much more so, then, idle chatter?

Furthermore, he is free from covetousness. Regarding the possessions, wealth, and requisites of others, which are held by others, he does not even give rise to a longing for them; how much less so the thought, "May what belongs to others become mine"? He does not crave it, he does not direct his mind toward it, and he does not give rise to a heart of greed.

Furthermore, he is indeed one whose mind is free from malice toward all sentient beings; his mind is one of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, a mind of compassion, a mind of happiness, and a gentle mind; his mind is intent on favoring the entire world and possesses a mind of sympathy for the welfare of all sentient beings. He [abandons] those things such as anger, enmity, stubbornness, impurity, ill-will, and torment...
Having abandoned those thoughts associated with resentment and the like that have been kindled by laughter,
he becomes one who reflects upon and cultivates those thoughts which are associated with benefit, associated with loving-kindness, and intended for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, one who possesses right view has indeed entered upon the correct path; he is free from curiosity, auspicious rites, and various kinds of unwholesome views; he is straight in vision, honest, and without deceit; and his intention is fixed upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and so forth.

Therein, one accomplishes the first three wholesome paths of action by means of the body; the middle four by means of speech; and the final three by means of the mind. In this way, one accumulates all ten wholesome paths of action.
Furthermore, does a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of enlightenment not accumulate these paths of action?
He too accumulates them; however, all ten of these are wholesome paths.
These become more abundant and purer for him than they are for a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening.
Through his tranquility and his radiance,
he always shines, perfectly pure like the moon in autumn.

Tranquility is the restraint of the senses; radiance is the luminosity of the body. If one who possesses such perfectly pure conduct were to perceive a self-nature within that purity of conduct, then he would not be one of pure conduct.

As it is said in the *Ārya-ratnakūṭa-sūtra*: "In this regard, Kāśyapa, a certain monk is virtuous; he is restrained by the vows of the Prātimokṣa, perfected in conduct and sphere of activity, seeing danger even in the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the precepts. He is pure in body, speech, and mind..."

He is endowed with [proper] conduct; his livelihood is pure; and he becomes one who speaks of a self. Kāśyapa, this is the first type of immoral person who merely resembles one possessed of morality. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose here a certain monk, having undertaken the twelve ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), dwells [in them]. Upala—
And he possesses false views; he abides in the notions of "I" and "mine. Kāśyapa, this is the fourth type of one who is immoral yet appears to be virtuous.
Therefore, he is always perfectly established in the three [jewels], his mental activity being free from the two types of inferiority.
Regarding those beings from whom one abstains, the one who abstains, and that which is abstained from— in all three of these,
one becomes free from the dualistic cognition of existence and non-existence.

Having thus demonstrated the possession of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlasampad*) by Bodhisattvas in general, [the author], wishing to establish hereafter that for others as well the perfection of ethical discipline is of even greater magnitude than giving (*dāna*) and the other perfections, and is the foundation for all attainments of virtuous qualities, says:
Through generosity, even a being who has stumbled in the practice of ethical conduct may obtain enjoyments even in an unfortunate rebirth;
for it is precisely because of that very generosity that this virtuous person becomes a master of giving among the distinguished gods and humans.

The arising of an abundance of enjoyments. Precisely because of this, even for one who has fallen into a state of miserable rebirth due to a lapse in the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*), having been born among the various hells, or among ghosts (*preta*) possessing great supernatural powers (*maharddhika*), such as individual hell-beings (*pratyekanaraka*), cattle, horses, elephants, monkeys, and nāgas, there will indeed be the arising of a manifold abundance of enjoyments. And from that, [the following occurs].
And because of the complete exhaustion of the root of acquisition, his enjoyments would not arise again.

For he who, having obtained the arising of a vast harvest from the sowing of a very small seed, sows even more abundant seed than that for the sake of further fruit—for him, a great accumulation of fruit is expected, with its sequence uninterrupted as it increases over time. But he who... [the previous] ancient... (Note: The provided source text was cut off; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Out of dullness, one who acts with ingratitude consumes only the seed; since even the original capital, along with its interest, has been exhausted by greed, how can there be any future accumulation of the fruit?

Thus, for one who lacks ethical discipline (*śīla*) and consequently enjoys wealth in an improper manner, the further projection of new wealth is impossible due to extreme sluggishness; and because all previously projected wealth has been consumed, the arising of further enjoyments cannot be expected. Moreover, it is not only the accomplishment of the arising of enjoyments that is exceedingly difficult for such a person, but also [the attainment of] that which is devoid of the sequence of ethical discipline.

Demonstrating that even the emergence of one who has fallen into an evil state (apāya) is exceedingly difficult to achieve, he says: "If this [being], whose activity is independent and who remains in equilibrium, does not sustain himself at that time, then, having fallen into dependence on others, by what means shall he ever rise up again?"

This [being], whose conduct was previously independent by its own will and who was established in the destinies of gods, humans, and so forth, now remains like a released prisoner confined to a single spot; if this hero does not sustain himself at that time, then having fallen into ruin and being cast like a captive into the vast mountain caves of the lower realms, by what means indeed shall he ever rise up again?
By falling away from that very state, he inevitably incurs the status of a resident [of hell]. Therefore it has been said:
"If, however, he is reborn among humans, he brings about two types of maturation."

And since immorality is thus the locus for the accumulation of so many faults, the Jina, having delivered a discourse on generosity, proceeded to deliver discourses concerning the sequence of ethical discipline (*śīla*). For this very reason, immediately after the time of the discourse on generosity, the Jina—who has conquered all unwholesome phenomena—[proceeded with... dā-
He delivered discourses on ethical discipline alone for the sake of ensuring that virtues such as *nādi* are not lost;
for it is only upon the ground of ethical discipline that virtues flourish and yield their fruits in an uninterrupted succession.
Because it is the foundation for all virtuous qualities, ethical discipline (*śīla*) alone is the earth. Upon it, virtues such as generosity and the rest flourish;
through a continuous succession of causes and effects in an ever-increasing sequence, they accumulate a mass of fruit that can be enjoyed for a long time. It is not otherwise.
Therefore, by this principle,
for ordinary worldlings, for those who have heard the Dharma, for those whose nature is fixed in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
and for the sons of the Victors, there is nothing superior to ethical discipline for the sake of the highest good and for worldly prosperity.

As it has been said: "Because the undertaking of these ten unwholesome paths of action is excessive, it is the cause for rebirth in hell; because it is moderate, it is the cause for rebirth as an animal; because it is slight, it is the cause for the world of Yama. Among them, the taking of life leads to hell, leads to rebirth as an animal, and leads to the world of Yama."
...leads [one] to rebirth. Furthermore, if one is reborn among humans, two results are produced:
a short lifespan and much illness. Taking what is not given leads to rebirth in hell, and so on, up to meager wealth and having to share one's wealth with others. Sexual misconduct leads to hell—

False speech leads one to hell, up to a state of having an unrefined retinue and having a wife with rivals. Slander leads one to hell, up to a state of being frequently slandered by others and being separated from one's retinue, as well as having an inferior...

And malicious speech leads to hell, up to the state of hearing what is unpleasant and an abundance of quarreling. Frivolous chatter leads to hell, up to the state of one whose words are not accepted and whose speech is indecisive. Covetousness leads to hell, up to...

Lack of contentment and great desire lead to hell, as do malice, lack of benevolence, and the intent to oppress others. False view leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, and leads to the world of Yama. Furthermore, if one is reborn among humans, two [consequences follow]...
He brings about maturation— being fallen into wrong views, deceitful, and full of guile. In this way, indeed,
these ten unwholesome paths of action lead to the origination of a great and immeasurable mass of suffering.

Furthermore, by virtue of undertaking the ten wholesome paths of action, the spheres of rebirth are known to extend from birth as a human being up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Beyond that, these same ten wholesome paths of action, when cultivated through the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*), become [the basis for] the limited...

Because their minds are thus bound to the three realms, because they lack great compassion, and because they follow what is heard from others and follow the sound [of the teachings], they bring about the Śrāvaka vehicle. Subsequently, having been purified, because they are not led by others and because it is conducive to self-becoming, they attain self-enlightenment.

That which, by not seeking from others, by being devoid of the skillful means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and by the realization of profound dependent origination (*idampratyayatā*), leads to the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddhas*; but beyond that, when it is further purified by way of a vast and immeasurable mind, endowed with great compassion, and embraced by skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*)—

"By that well-established great vow, by the non-abandonment of all sentient beings, and by having the vast cognitive domain of the Buddha's wisdom as its object, they lead to the expansion of the conduct that purifies all the bodhisattva stages and the perfections," and so forth.

Therefore, by this reasoning, having set aside these ten paths of wholesome action, there is no other means for the attainment of the prosperity consisting of worldly happiness— as it occurs for ordinary persons, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas— and of the ultimate good characterized by liberation, which is by nature neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
It is clearly demonstrated that there is generally no [such thing]. As for this bodhisattva who has generated the second thought of enlightenment,
he is like the ocean [which cannot coexist] with a corpse.
Just as Lakṣmī does not desire to dwell with Kālakarṇī, so the high-souled one, established in superior virtue, does not seek residence together with its failure.
It is a synonym for the misfortune of Kālakarṇī.

He explains the classification of the perfections (pāramitā) regarding the aforementioned ethical discipline (śīla): "That [act], that [person], and from those [objects]— when there is the apprehension of these three, it is indeed called 'abstinence' (virati) in its etymological sense."
This is called a mundane perfection because it is a morality that exists when there is the apprehension of these three;
it is supramundane when it is empty of attachment to those three.
When there is the non-apprehension of the aforementioned triad, that very ethical discipline is said to be the supramundane perfection.

Concluding the section on the perfection of ethical discipline by way of restating the qualities of the stages as they have been described: This splendor of existence arising from the moon that is the Son of the Victor— pure and free from stains, just like the moonlight of the autumnal night— removes the fever of the minds of people.

"Stainless" refers to the second bodhisattva stage, which is so named because it arises from the meaning of the stainlessness of the ten paths of wholesome action. Just as the moonlight of the autumn moon, free from impurity, removes the heat of people during the summer, so too does this "Stainless" stage, produced by the moon that is the Son of the Conqueror, remove the affliction of evil...

It removes the mental torment born of moral failure. Furthermore, it is non-becoming (*abhava*), because it is not included within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Moreover, it is the glory of becoming (*bhavaśrī*), because all perfections of virtue are dependent upon it and because it is the cause for the perfection of sovereignty over the four continents.
In the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, the second generation of the mind of enlightenment, named "The Stainless."

Now, with reference to the third production of the thought of awakening, he says: This is the third stage, the Radiant (prabhākarī), because of the arising of light from the fire that burns the fuel of all the factors of enlightenment without remainder.

"Prabhākarī" is the name of the third bodhisattva stage. Why, then, is this called "Prabhākarī"? To demonstrate its etymological significance: because the light of the fire of gnosis—which is quiescent in nature and consumes the fuel of all objects of knowledge without exception—arises in this stage, this stage is designated as Prabhākarī. Of that third...
The radiance of this son of the Sugata, who has generated that resolve, is like copper or like the sun.

For just as the copper-colored glow of the sun arises in its state prior to sunrise, even so does the radiance of wisdom arise for the Bodhisattva in this stage. And regarding that Bodhisattva who has thus attained the radiance of wisdom, [the author], demonstrating the preeminence of his perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), says:
Even if someone were to unreasonably cut the flesh from his body, piece by piece with a razor, along with the bones, for a very long time; even then—
For one who cuts [a tree], his merit becomes even greater through forgiveness.

Because he protects the minds of others and because of the presence of such knowledge, the bodhisattva does not manifest any such activity of body, speech, or mind that would become a basis for resentment in others who fear harm throughout the three times; therefore, it is specified as follows:
"Even if someone were to cause him no offense"—

if even such a person were to take the flesh from the body of that Bodhisattva along with the bone, and were to cut it into pieces for a very long time, resting repeatedly; even if [the opponent] were of such a kind...

Not only does a mind of malice not arise in the Bodhisattva toward the one who cuts him, but rather, even greater forbearance arises in him as he contemplates the suffering of the hells and other realms resulting from that evil deed.
For a Bodhisattva who perceives the absence of self, what could be cut, by what, when, or how? Since he has seen all phenomena as being like reflections, he therefore practices patience.

Not only does he endure the sufferings of hell and so forth, which have their cause in those evil deeds, with extreme patience; but because he has seen all phenomena as being like reflections, he endures them even more thoroughly due to the disappearance of the notions of "self" and "mine. The word "and" (ca) serves to collect the causes of forbearance.

The meaning is this: patience is not merely a quality arising from Bodhisattvas; it is also the cause for protecting the entire collection of virtues in others. To turn away those who are full of resentment and envy, he states the following reasoning:
If remorse arises after an injury has been committed, what is gained by that remorse?
It is surely useless here, and in the next world it will certainly lead to adverse results.

If, first of all, this person becomes angry with another who has done him harm because that anger provides an opening for resentment, then, since the harm already done cannot be undone, the arising of distress based upon it is entirely purposeless; for what was destined to happen has already occurred. Not only is the arising of his distress purposeless at that time, [but it is also unproductive].
Furthermore, the next world is contradicted [by this view], because when resentment arises, it projects an undesirable karmic maturation.
Even for one who is currently experiencing the remainder of the maturation of the fruit of his own past misconduct, if— out of delusion—
he imagines that another is harming him and thus feels distress toward that wrongdoer, he will respond with retaliation.

And because of this, there arises a desire to retaliate against those who have done one harm; warding that off as well, he says: "How indeed can that very thing which is intended to be the fruit of previously committed unwholesome karma—the fruit that brings about its own exhaustion—be turned into a seed for further suffering by means of harming others and through anger?"
Even this great slaughter and injury to his body, brought about by enemies through the falling of sharp sword-blades,

is but the remaining *niṣyanda-phala* (outflowing fruit) of previously committed acts such as taking life, which have already yielded their extremely intense ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*) experienced in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama.

The final emergence of the fruit is the cause for the cessation of all unwanted results of the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) without exception. How could that [final fruit] be the cause for an emergence of fruit that— like the drinking of a final medicine which causes the departure of a disease already within the stomach— is even more harmful than the unwanted result it has already transcended through its transformation?

Since one should not be led away by anger or the desire to harm others, it is therefore proper to endure with even greater fortitude that which causes the arising of immediate suffering, as it is the cause for the removal of disease— just like a physician who performs surgery with a sharp instrument.
Envy is not only the cause for projecting an undesirable and vast karmic maturation according to the reasoning already described;
it is also the cause for the exhaustion of a long-accumulated store of merit. Demonstrating this, he says:
"For impatience destroys the merit acquired over hundreds of eons through both generosity and ethical discipline."
Because for even a single moment, there is no evil greater than impatience toward the sons of the Victors.
Because he lacks the discernment to distinguish between different types of persons, even if he does possess such discernment, his conduct remains dependent on the habitual practice of afflictions;

thus, if he were to harbor a mind of resentment— even for a single moment— toward those who have generated the thought of awakening, by falsely imputing real or unreal faults upon them, he would thereby destroy the mass of merit accumulated over hundreds of eons.

One would destroy even one who is supreme in the practice of the perfections of generosity and ethical discipline; even a Mahābodhisattva. How much more so a non-Bodhisattva toward Bodhisattvas? Here, the limit of the karmic maturation cannot be determined, just as the measure of the water in the great ocean cannot be calculated by the number of *pala*s. Thus it is.

There is no other sin more excellent than impatience (akṣamā) in its projection of undesirable karmic fruition and its destruction of merit. For it was said by the Blessed One: "O Mañjuśrī, 'anger, anger'—it destroys the merit accumulated over hundreds of thousands of eons; therefore it is called 'anger'."
Moreover, this intolerance, when directed toward those incapable of harming others, destroys only oneself;
yet when directed toward the powerful and merciless, it strikes down both oneself and others.
It brings about ruin at its very inception, leads to deformity and wickedness, and robs one of the discernment that distinguishes between right and wrong conduct.
But later, by abandoning the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), impatience will cause one to fall swiftly into an evil rebirth.
If these are the faults of impatience, what then are the virtues of its opposite, patience? To this he says:
Forgiveness, however, produces the virtues that are contrary to those [previously mentioned].
He is gracious, beloved by virtuous people, and skilled in discerning right from wrong conduct;
beyond this, through endurance, there shall be birth among gods and humans and the destruction of unwholesome karma.
Whatever faults have been described regarding intolerance, these should be understood as the virtues of forbearance, which is its opposite.

Having understood the faults and virtues of anger and forbearance, both the ordinary person and the son of the Conqueror should swiftly abandon intolerance and always practice patience, which is praised by the noble ones.

*Roṣaśca kṣamā ca* means anger and forbearance; *doṣāśca guṇāśca* means faults and virtues; and *roṣakṣamayor doṣaguṇāḥ* is the analysis of the compound. Having understood the faults of anger as they have been described, and having recognized the virtues of forbearance through their opposite, one should abandon forbearance [only when it is misplaced] and practice forbearance alone at all times.

Now, demonstrating the classification of the perfections (*pāramitā*) with respect to patience (*kṣamā*), he says: When there is apprehension (*upalambha*) of the triad—that which endures, that which endures, and those beings toward whom one endures—even though it is dedicated toward the enlightenment of a perfectly awakened Buddha, this [patience] is mundane. This refers to the triad...
When there is apprehension of this [object], even this patience dedicated toward buddhahood is called the mundane perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
The Buddhas declare that very same perfection to be supramundane when it is without apprehension.

And just as the perfection of patience becomes purified for the Bodhisattva on this stage, so too on this ground the meditations and superknowledges belong to the Son of the Buddha, and there is the complete destruction of passion and hatred. On this stage, he is constantly capable of destroying the passion for sense-pleasures of the world.
Regarding the term "meditations" (*dhyānāni*), the word "meditation" is used as an illustration; it includes the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) as well.

As it is stated in the *Third Bodhisattva Stage*: "That bodhisattva, established in this *Prabhākari* bodhisattva stage, [dwells] secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states..."

Having attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion; he, through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, and through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind,
attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and characterized by the joy and happiness born of concentration.

He dwells; through detachment from joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body— of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness, equanimous and mindful"— and thus he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which is free from joy.

Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental joy and mental grief, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness; these are the four dhyānas.

There are four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). They are as follows: by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," he, having attained the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), dwells therein. He, completely...

By transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He...
By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, one attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; these are the four formless attainments.

The four immeasurables are as follows: with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness— vast, exalted, non-dual, independent, immeasurable, free from enmity, without rivalry, unobstructed, and harmless— he pervades the entire world, which is as far-reaching as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and extends to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*).

Having pervaded the world and attained it, he dwells therein; likewise with a mind accompanied by compassion, accompanied by sympathetic joy, and accompanied by equanimity—extensive, as described before.

The five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). They are as follows: he experiences various kinds of miraculous powers (*ṛddhividhi*); he causes even the earth to tremble; having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one;
he experiences manifestation and disappearance; [he passes] through walls, through enclosures...
He travels unhindered through walls, just as if through space;

he moves cross-legged through the air, just like a winged bird; he performs the act of emerging and submerging in the earth, just as if in water; and he walks upon water without sinking, just as if on land.

On the earth, he smokes and even blazes up like a great mass of fire; yet he also emits water from his body like a great cloud, with which he extinguishes the conflagration of the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system. These two...
He touches and strokes with his hand even the moon and sun, so powerful and so majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world— this is the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhyabhijñā*).
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—
divine and human, subtle and gross, whether they are far or near—
even to the point of hearing the sounds of gadflies, mosquitoes, insects, and birds.
Thus ends the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear.
Having pervaded the minds of other beings and other persons with his own mind, he understands them as they truly are. He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" as it truly is;
he understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" as it truly is. Likewise, [he understands] a mind with hatred...

He understands, as it truly is, the mind free from corruption as "the mind free from corruption," the deluded mind as "deluded," the mind free from delusion as "free from delusion," the afflicted mind as "afflicted," the unafflicted mind as "unafflicted," the limited mind as "limited," the expansive mind as "expansive," the vast mind as "vast," the immeasurable mind as "immeasurable," the contracted mind as "contracted," the distracted mind as "distracted," the concentrated mind as "concentrated," the unconcentrated mind as "unconcentrated," the liberated mind as "liberated," the unliberated mind as "unliberated," the blemished mind as "blemished," the unblemished mind as "unblemished," and the gross mind as "gross.
He understands the gross mind as "gross mind" according to reality.
"He understands as it really is a non-gross mind as 'a non-gross mind'—
for he understands the mind of other beings, of other persons, with his own mind as it really is. This is the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of others' minds (*paracittajñānābhijñā*).
He recollects his manifold past abodes; he recollects even one birth, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty,
a hundred births, a thousand births, many hundreds of births, and many thousands of births.

He recollects many thousands of births, even many hundreds of thousands of births, even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of births; he recollects an eon of dissolution, an eon of evolution,
an eon of both dissolution and evolution, and even many such eons of dissolution and evolution.

He recollects one eon; he recollects even a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, and even a thousand million eons; indeed, he recollects many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. "I was such-and-such a person, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, and such a complexion."

Thus he recollects his manifold former abodes with their modes, their causes, and their details: "I had such a physical appearance, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such experiences of pleasure and pain; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; and passing away from there, I was reborn here. This is the recollection of former abodes.
That is the supernormal knowledge of recollection.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings— passing away and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, lowly and exalted—
and he understands beings as they truly are according to their karma: "These, sirs, are beings..."

Endowed with misconduct of body, endowed with misconduct of speech, and endowed with misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views— on account of their undertaking actions based on wrong views, and by reason of that cause and condition, after the breaking up of the body, following death, [they go] to a state of woe...

Those who fall into the miserable states and are reborn in the hells; whereas these beings, moreover, are endowed with good conduct of body, up to not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and because of undertaking actions based on right view— for that cause and for that condition, after the dissolution of the body, [they go to a good destination].

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees all beings— how they pass away from death and are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world among the gods— with their forms, their details, and their causes;
he sees them passing away and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, even unto their states according to their karma.
He understands reality as it truly is.
He enters into and emerges from these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), absorptions (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).

Yet, he is not reborn under their influence; rather, wherever he perceives the fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), there he is intentionally reborn by the power of his vow. For what reason? Because—
For the mental continuum of that bodhisattva has been brought forth through skill in means.

In this way, on this stage, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) arise for the bodhisattva. How does the complete exhaustion of passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) occur? The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; thus, there also occurs for him the complete exhaustion of delusion (*moha*).
How so? This too is according to the Sūtra, as it was said: [regarding] all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
He contemplates non-transmigration and non-destruction through the principle of dependent origination;
for him, to a still greater degree, all bonds of desire do not exist here, nor all bonds of hatred,
nor all bonds of form, nor all bonds of ignorance.
The fetters of speculative views have already been abandoned by him.
For that bodhisattva established on this *prabhākārī* bodhisattva-ground, there are many hundreds of kalpas,
many thousands of kalpas, and many hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

For many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, for many tens of millions of eons, up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, there occurs a non-increase and the abandonment of false passion; a non-increase and the abandonment of false hatred; a non-increase and the abandonment of false delusion...
He goes toward the abandonment of [the defilements]; thus, there comes about the complete destruction of his passion, hatred, and delusion.
He is constantly capable of destroying the passion for sensual desire in the world.

As it has been said: "In this regard, O sons of the Conqueror, there is the third bodhisattva stage of the bodhisattva called *Prabhākarī* (The Luminous), by which he is designated. Established in this stage, the bodhisattva for the most part becomes Indra, the king of the gods, the lord of the thirty-three, skillful and powerful."

He is skilled in applying the means for turning back sensual desire among beings so as to lift them out from the mire of desire; thus this son of the Conqueror becomes capable of destroying sensual desire in the world. In this way, this bodhisattva, on the third bodhisattva stage, [attains] patience—

He necessarily attains the complete purification of the perfections, the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the attainments, and the superknowledges, as well as the total destruction of passion and the other afflictions.

Now, illustrating the establishment of the excellence of the basis, the equipment, the intrinsic nature, and the perfection of the fruit for the triad of perfections culminating in the perfection of patience, he says:
"These three qualities beginning with generosity are generally praised by the Sugata for householders."
