And this accumulation, known as merit, is the cause for the body whose nature is the form of a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Although only Bodhisattvas are the basis for the practices such as giving as they have been described, nevertheless, this is stated with reference to the possibility of these two paths—lay and monastic—existing among them. Among those, for laypeople, these three qualities beginning with giving are generally easy to accomplish, whereas for those who have gone forth, they are vigor, meditation, and wisdom. Not...

For others, however, the other [accumulation] is not possible. There are two accumulations that are the cause of Buddhahood, namely, the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) and the accumulation of knowledge (*jñānasaṃbhāra*). In this regard, the accumulation of merit consists of these three perfections (*pāramitā*); the accumulation of knowledge consists of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). However, vigor (*vīrya*) is established as the cause for both.

In this regard, that which is the accumulation of merit is the cause of the form-body (rūpakāya) of the Blessed Buddhas— a body that possesses the hundred marks of merit, is marvelous, inconceivable, and manifold in form. However, the accumulation of gnosis is the cause of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which is characterized by non-arising.
Now, having manifested the majesty [of this stage] through the majesty of its basis and so forth, he speaks as follows, concluding the section on the third bodhisattva stage:
"Having first thoroughly dispelled the darkness within himself, he desires to strike down the darkness of the world."
O Sun among the Sons of the Victors,

this Radiant Stage (Prabhākarī) belonging to the Sons of the Sugatas remains here; having dispelled at the very moment of its arising the ignorance residing within its own basis— which acts as an obstacle to its own production— it desires [to dispel] that of others.
By giving such instruction, he destroys the darkness that obstructs the arising of the third stage;
and this Bodhisattva,
though even more sharp-witted here on earth, does not fall into anger.

Like the sun, which destroys the darkness of faults that impair virtues, he does not become angry even with people who possess faults, despite his exceedingly sharp conduct; this is because of his practice of extreme forbearance and because his mental continuum is moistened by compassion.
In the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, this is the third generation of the mind of awakening, called "The Radiant."

Now, by highlighting the superiority of the perfection of vigor over the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, he speaks with reference to the fourth production of the thought of awakening:
"All qualities without exception are consequent upon vigor; it is the cause of both accumulations, namely merit and wisdom."
For that upon which vigor attains its brilliance is this fourth stage, the Radiant.

For one who lacks enthusiasm for wholesome action, there is an absolute absence of engagement in giving and the like, and thus the arising of all virtues is impossible. However, for one who possesses enthusiasm, because there is the possibility of increasing and attaining both previously acquired and unattained virtues, vigor alone is the cause of all virtues. [This explains] the state of being the cause of the two accumulations.

This has already been explained. That earth upon which this vigor bears a brilliance even greater due to the purification of its own qualities is this fourth bodhisattva stage, named Arciṣmatī (The Radiant).
Why, then, is this called "The Radiant" (*arciṣmatī*)? Elucidating the cause for the application of this designation, he says:
"The radiance is superior to the copper-like glow, arising from the superior cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment."

Because in this [ground] there arises for the son of the Sugata a radiance superior to the previously mentioned copper-colored radiance resulting from the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) on this stage of the Bodhisattva, it is therefore called *Samyagājāti*.
Because of the arising of the flames of the fire of gnosis, this bodhisattva stage is named Arciṣmatī (The Radiant).
In that regard, there are thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),

the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), and the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

In that regard, there are the four foundations of mindfulness. As it has been said: "Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, that bodhisattva, being established in this Radiant Bodhisattva-ground, dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful."

Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, he dwells observing the body in the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. "Observing the body in the internal and external body" is as before. Likewise with regard to internal feelings, and—

He dwells observing internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings; he dwells observing the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds—as described previously. He dwells observing internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
Thus is the detailed exposition.

The four right efforts are as follows: for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and correctly applies himself. For the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen...

"For the abandoning of unwholesome states," as before; "for the arising of unarisen wholesome states," as before; "for the stability, non-confusion, expansion, increase, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire and exerts himself."
Thus, as before.

The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): namely, he cultivates the base of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. Likewise, [he cultivates] the base of psychic power endowed with the concentration of energy and the formative forces of abandonment...

He cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and the concentration of mind, as before; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and the concentration of investigation, as before.

The five faculties, namely: he cultivates the faculty of faith based on seclusion, and so forth; likewise, he cultivates the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom based on seclusion and based on dispassion, and so on.
The five powers are those same [five faculties] when their opposing factors have been conquered, as described previously.

The seven factors of enlightenment, namely: he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, and so forth; likewise, the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment that is energy, the factor of enlightenment that is joy, the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, the factor of enlightenment that is concentration, and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.
He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is based on seclusion, as described previously.

The noble eightfold path, namely: one cultivates right view, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; one cultivates right intention, as before; [and] right speech, right action, right livelihood, and—
He cultivates right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, based on seclusion, as described previously.
On this stage, not only does the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment arise,
but there is also the complete exhaustion of contact with one's own [wrong] views.
On this very stage, the destruction of his own false views arises, as it has been said: "Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, for that Bodhisattva who stands on this Radiant Bodhisattva stage,
those [views] preceded by the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)— namely, the notions of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person..."

All those flashings and blinkings, discursive thoughts and deliberations, cherished possessions, things clung to as "mine," objects of wealth, and bases of attachment that arise from the adherence to the person, the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields— all these have departed from him.
In the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, this is the fourth generation of the mind of awakening, called "The Radiant."
Now, with reference to the fifth production of the thought of enlightenment, it is said:
That Great Being, established in the fifth bodhisattva stage, Durjayā (Difficult to Conquer), cannot be defeated even by all the Māras on earth; [he is] situated in all the world-systems.
Even those sons of the gods who are Māras are unable to conquer him, let alone others such as the servants of Māra;

for this very reason, this stage is named "The Very Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā). Furthermore, this Bodhisattva should be understood as one who excels in meditative concentration (dhyāna) and has attained supreme skill even in the awakening to the subtle nature of reality through right understanding.

Among the ten perfections, the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) arises as preeminent for him. "Those with right understanding" refers to the noble ones (*āryas*). The meaning is that the truths of those who possess right understanding are the "truths of right understanding," which are the noble truths (*āryasatyas*). "Own-form" (*svarūpa*) means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Own-form that is accessible through subtle knowledge is "subtle own-form. That—

Great skill arises in him for thoroughly understanding the subtle nature of the truths of cognition. In that regard, there are four noble truths known as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. But is it not the case that only two truths were taught by the Blessed One, namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)? As it has been said:
In the *Pitāputrasamāgamasūtra*:
"The Knower of the World has himself taught these two truths, without having heard them from others:
the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and likewise the ultimate (*paramārtha*). There exists no third truth."
Thus:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning."

Thus [it is asked]: "Why is that? For apart from the two truths, there are no other four noble truths. To this he says: "Even though it is so, nevertheless, the four noble truths are taught here for the purpose of demonstrating the individual relationship between cause and effect regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. Among these, the category of what is to be abandoned is affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Its fruit..."
The truth of suffering; the truth of origin as its cause; purification as the category of what is to be adopted;

its fruit is the truth of cessation; and the means for attaining that is the truth of the path. Among these, the truths of suffering, origin, and the path are included within conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya); the nature of the truth of cessation is ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
True; likewise, whatever other collection of truths exists, that too should be understood as being included within the two truths, according to the circumstances.

But is there any other truth besides the four noble truths? He says that there is, as it is stated in the *Pañcamī Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "One understands, as it truly is, 'This is the noble truth of suffering'; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

He understands, as it truly is, that "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to cessation. In this way, he becomes skilled in conventional truth, skilled in ultimate truth, skilled in the truth of characteristics,
skilled in the truth of classification, and skilled in the truth of thorough investigation.

He is skilled in the truth of entities, skilled in the truth of origination, skilled in the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, and skilled in the truth of entering the knowledge of the path. Through the accomplishment of the continuity of all bodhisattva activities, he becomes skilled in the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s knowledge as well. He, for others—

By satisfying beings according to their inclinations, one understands conventional truth; by the convergence into a single principle, one understands ultimate truth; by the realization of specific and general characteristics, one understands the truth of characteristics;
and by the realization of the establishment of the classification of phenomena, one understands the truth of differentiation.
Through the realization of the establishment of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one understands the truth of exhaustion (*nistīraṇasatya*).

Because it consists of the onset of afflictions that torment the body and mind, one understands the truth of the factual (*vastusatya*). Because of the connection with the transition between states of existence (*gati*), one understands the truth of origination (*prabhavasatya*). [It is] the absolute cessation of all fevers and torments...

Through tranquility (*śama*), one understands the truth of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising; through the accomplishment of non-duality, one understands the truth of entering the knowledge of the path; and through the complete awakening to all aspects, by way of accomplishing the continuity of activities on all the bodhisattva stages up to the arising of the knowledge of a Tathāgata, one understands the truth.
Thus it is said.
In the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, this is the fifth generation of the mind of awakening, called "Very Difficult to Conquer."
